title: Career Roadmap · HPC Engineer
summary: An HPC Engineer designs, configures, operates and optimizes computing systems that solve problems requiring substantial computational power. These systems may contain hundreds or thousands of CPU cores, GPUs, high-speed interconnects and shared storage.

facts.Current degree: B.Tech / B.E. in Computational Engineering / Computational Science

about.label: Industry
about.text: Scientific computing, AI infrastructure, aerospace, climate modelling, engineering simulation, research computing

about.label: Core Focus
about.text: Parallel computing, cluster architecture, performance optimization, distributed workloads and scientific software

about.label: Career Outlook
about.text: Specialized career supporting computationally intensive workloads across research, engineering and AI infrastructure

blocks.text: An HPC Engineer designs, configures, operates and optimizes computing systems that solve problems requiring substantial computational power. These systems may contain hundreds or thousands of CPU cores, GPUs, high-speed interconnects and shared storage.

HPC engineers help researchers and engineering teams run workloads such as weather forecasting, computational fluid dynamics, molecular simulation, seismic analysis, large-scale numerical modelling and scientific AI.
The role combines systems engineering, Linux administration, programming, parallel algorithms, networking, storage and performance analysis.

blocks.label: Recommended starting focus
blocks.text: Linux, C/C++, Python, computer architecture, parallel programming with OpenMP and MPI, and job scheduling on compute clusters.

rows.text: Continued use of CPU/GPU clusters, cloud HPC, containerized workloads and optimized scientific computing
Greater integration of AI and simulation workloads, heterogeneous computing and energy-aware scheduling
Potential advances in specialized accelerators, scalable scientific workflows and automated performance optimization
Possible expansion of new computing architectures and increasingly integrated simulation-and-AI platforms

blocks.text: These are indicative technology trends, not guaranteed employment or salary forecasts.
Year 1 — Computing and Mathematics Foundations

blocks.label: Primary objective
blocks.text: Build a strong foundation in programming, mathematics and computer systems.

rows.text: Calculus, linear algebra, probability and differential equations
Arrays, linked lists, trees, graphs and algorithmic complexity
CPU, memory, storage, operating systems and computer architecture
Shell commands, filesystem, processes, permissions and scripting
Floating-point arithmetic, numerical errors and basic numerical algorithms

blocks.text: Projects

items.text: Implement matrix multiplication in C and Python.
Compare execution times for different sorting and numerical algorithms.
Write a command-line tool to monitor CPU and memory usage.
Implement a basic numerical solver for a mathematical problem.

blocks.label: Milestone
blocks.text: Understand how algorithms interact with hardware and how to measure program performance.
Year 2 — Parallel Programming and Operating Systems

blocks.label: Primary objective
blocks.text: Learn how computational tasks can execute concurrently across multiple CPU cores.

rows.text: Processes, threads, memory management and synchronization
Multithreading, race conditions, locks and barriers
Message passing across processes and compute nodes
Cache hierarchy, memory bandwidth and vectorization
Parallel reduction, sorting and numerical algorithms

blocks.text: Projects

items.text: Parallelize matrix multiplication using OpenMP.
Implement numerical integration using MPI.
Compare sequential and parallel implementations of a numerical algorithm.
Analyze the impact of thread count and workload size on execution time.

blocks.label: Milestone
blocks.text: Understand the difference between shared-memory and distributed-memory parallelism.
Year 3 — Cluster Computing and Performance Engineering

blocks.label: Primary objective
blocks.text: Learn how to deploy, manage and optimize workloads on multi-node computing systems.

rows.text: Compute nodes, head/login nodes, networking and shared storage
Slurm, job queues, resource requests and scheduling policies
MPI collectives, communication costs and scaling
CUDA fundamentals or another available accelerator programming environment
Parallel I/O, data locality and high-throughput storage
Profiling, bottleneck analysis and memory optimization
Numerical simulation, linear algebra and iterative solvers
Reproducible environments using suitable container technologies

blocks.text: Major projects

items.text: Build a small multi-node MPI application where cluster access is available.
Create Slurm job scripts for CPU-based scientific workloads.
Benchmark a parallel matrix solver and analyze its scaling behaviour.
Accelerate a numerical kernel using GPU computing where suitable hardware is available.

blocks.label: Milestone
blocks.text: Run and optimize a workload using realistic resource limits, performance metrics and reproducible execution steps.
Year 4 — Advanced HPC and Industry Readiness
For a three-year degree, adapt these activities to the final year or final two semesters.

blocks.label: Primary objective
blocks.text: Develop an HPC specialization and complete a reproducible, performance-focused capstone.

rows.text: Hybrid MPI + OpenMP and workload decomposition
Strong scaling, weak scaling, profiling and bottleneck identification
Resource allocation, monitoring, software environments and troubleshooting
Memory transfers, kernel profiling and accelerator utilization
Failure handling, checkpoint/restart and workload recovery
Develop and benchmark a parallel scientific application
Research computing internship, cluster project or technical portfolio

blocks.label: Recommended capstone
blocks.text: Performance Optimization of a Parallel Scientific Simulation on CPU and GPU Architectures.

Compare a sequential baseline with parallel implementations. Report execution time, speedup, parallel efficiency, memory use and, where available, energy consumption. Document the hardware and software configuration so that others can reproduce the results.
1. HPC Systems Engineer
Builds, configures and maintains compute clusters, scheduling systems, Linux environments and shared storage.

blocks.label: Core skills
blocks.text: Linux, cluster administration, Slurm, networking, monitoring and automation.
2. Parallel Computing Engineer
Develops software that distributes computational work across CPU cores and multiple nodes.

blocks.label: Core skills
blocks.text: C/C++, MPI, OpenMP, algorithms, synchronization and performance analysis.
3. GPU Computing Engineer
Optimizes computationally intensive applications for GPUs and heterogeneous computing systems.

blocks.label: Core skills
blocks.text: CUDA or equivalent frameworks, parallel algorithms, memory optimization and profiling.
4. Scientific Computing Engineer
Develops and optimizes numerical applications for physics, engineering, climate science and computational research.

blocks.label: Core skills
blocks.text: Numerical methods, linear algebra, C/C++, Python and scientific libraries.

blocks.label: Recommended starting point
blocks.text: Parallel computing with C/C++, MPI and OpenMP. Add Linux cluster administration if you prefer infrastructure, or GPU programming and numerical methods if you prefer application performance engineering.
Essential tools and technologies

rows.text: GPU programming on supported NVIDIA hardware

blocks.text: You do not need access to a supercomputer to begin. Many foundational projects can run on a personal computer, while cloud, university and national research computing facilities can provide access to larger systems when available.

rows.text: MPI, numerical methods and scaling analysis

blocks.text: For each project, include source code, build instructions, test cases, hardware specifications, benchmark methodology and measured results. Show both absolute performance and speedup; faster execution on one test does not automatically imply good scalability.

rows.text: Learn C/C++, Linux and basic computer architecture
Apply for research computing, systems programming, parallel computing or GPU internships
Complete a benchmark-driven capstone and seek cluster or scientific-computing experience
Publish a reproducible portfolio and practice systems-level interviews

blocks.text: Organizations and sectors to explore

items.text: Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) — high-performance computing, supercomputing systems and related software.
National Supercomputing Mission — relevant research-computing ecosystem and institutional opportunities.
Indian Institute of Science (IISc) — computational science and research computing.
Universities and national laboratories with scientific computing clusters.
Aerospace, automotive, semiconductor, climate modelling and engineering simulation companies.
Cloud computing and AI infrastructure providers.

blocks.text: Look for roles titled HPC Intern, Scientific Computing Intern, Parallel Programming Engineer Intern, Research Computing Assistant, Systems Software Intern and GPU Computing Intern. Current openings and eligibility vary by institution and employer.

rows.text: Support cluster users, jobs, software environments and troubleshooting
Automate, administer and troubleshoot Linux systems
Apply numerical methods to engineering and scientific problems

blocks.text: Some research-intensive roles may prefer a master's degree, particularly when they require advanced numerical modelling or specialized scientific knowledge.

rows.text: Cluster architecture, Linux, MPI, networking and performance analysis
Distributed workloads, containers, automation and resource optimization
Numerical methods, reproducible workflows and parallel programming
Computational fluid dynamics, structural simulation and performance engineering
Simulation workloads, numerical computing and compute infrastructure
GPUs, distributed computing, communication optimization and scheduling
Linux, job schedulers, scientific libraries and user support

blocks.text: Practical projects and measurable performance improvements are often more valuable than collecting certificates.

rows.text: CUDA or another supported accelerator framework
Numerical methods, BLAS/LAPACK and simulation techniques

blocks.text: Useful resources include the official OpenMP and MPI documentation, Slurm documentation, NVIDIA CUDA learning materials, Linux documentation and HPC training materials from research computing centers.
A postgraduate degree is not mandatory for every HPC engineering role, but it can improve access to advanced scientific computing, computational modelling and research-oriented positions.

blocks.label: GPU-accelerated computing
blocks.text: Increasing use of accelerators for simulation, AI and numerical workloads.

blocks.label: Heterogeneous computing

blocks.label: AI for scientific discovery

blocks.label: Energy-efficient computing

blocks.label: Cloud HPC
blocks.text: Provisioning scalable compute infrastructure for temporary or variable workloads.

blocks.label: Advanced interconnects
blocks.text: Faster communication between nodes and accelerators.

blocks.label: Quantum-classical integration
blocks.text: An emerging research area, not a replacement for conventional HPC in most current workloads.
A strong graduate candidate should be able to:

items.text: Write efficient C/C++ programs and debug memory or concurrency problems.
Use Linux and shell scripts to automate workflows.
Parallelize algorithms using OpenMP and MPI.
Submit and monitor batch jobs using a scheduler such as Slurm.
Profile programs and identify compute, memory or communication bottlenecks.
Explain speedup, parallel efficiency, strong scaling and weak scaling.
Understand GPU programming fundamentals.
Use scientific libraries and numerical methods appropriately.
Document reproducible benchmark results.
Troubleshoot basic cluster, job-execution and software-environment issues.

blocks.text: By graduation, aim to have three documented projects: one OpenMP application, one MPI application and one performance-optimization project. If possible, add GPU computing or practical experience using a shared research cluster.
